children: A decade after its enactment, the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code has reshaped corporate risk management, contracting, transaction structuring and distressed acquisitions. For general counsel, the evolving framework calls for early intervention, careful diligence and rigorous procedural compliance.
Teng Years of IBC: The General Counsel Perspective

As a transformative legislation, the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC) replaced the fragmented and unwieldy insolvency and recovery proceedings with a globally comparable framework, emphasising creditor-in-control, value preservation/maximisation, business continuity and time-bound resolutions. The IBC evolved over a decade through legislative amendments, including the latest IBC (Amendment) Act, 2026 (IBC 2.0) and striking judicial precedents.

According to figures published by the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI), till March 2026, 8,987 Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) have been admitted. While several cases were closed through settlements, appeals, reviews and withdrawals, creditors realised approximately ₹4.32 lakh crore through approved resolution plans and recoveries exceeded 94.56% of fair value.

Through the first decade of its implementation, IBC has reshaped corporate behaviour, from reactionary stance to proactive risk mitigation, credit management and strategic deal structuring. In-house counsels have played a tactical role in implementing this shift.
At the Point of Stress

Enterprise risk functions now treat IBC exposure as a board level matter, with early-warning systems and pre-admission settlement strategies getting heightened attention. A sound legal strategy at the initial point would be for a corporate to start considering Inter-Creditor Agreement, which allow lenders to restructure debt or implement a resolution plan outside the NCLT.

A proactive legal strategy would also include preventing the company from undertaking transactions that may later be challenged as ‘Preferential Transactions’ (Section 43), with a 2-years look back for related parties, ‘Undervalued Transactions’(Section 45) and/or ‘Fraudulent Trading’ (Section 66), where directors can face personal liability.
Counterparty Risk Management

Since IBC protects essential contracts, termination-on-insolvency clauses, netting rights and step-in provisions are now structured to hold up in an insolvency situation of the counterparty, such as escrow arrangements that keep cash outside the estate, direct agreements with lenders, and change-of-control language which includes a resolution applicant.
In
TCS v. Vishal Ghisulal Jain

(2021), the Supreme Court held that termination clause for insolvency cannot be invoked once the moratorium is in force, but termination for pre-existing, insolvency-unrelated breach stands. Legal professionals have also been considering most effective drafting of Material Adverse Change (MAC) provision in M&A and financing agreement, to guard against loss of rights upon CIRP commencement.
Transaction Structuring
ArcelorMittal India v. Satish Kumar Gupta

(2018) remains a key ruling for deal structuring. It gave "control" under Section 29A a wide, purposive meaning, allowed veil-piercing where group structures defeated public interest, and held that persons "connected" to a defaulting promoter cannot bid for the assets. This concept is aligned with global insolvency frameworks.
Alpha Corp Development v. GNIDA
(2026) revived that logic, lifting the veil between Earth Infrastructures and its subsidiaries to uphold resolution plans on the ground that inextricably connected group companies are one concern.

While advising on transaction, in-house counsels must bear in mind that a pure holding company, without substantial operations/business, relying solely on income from parent and sharing management team with parent company, may invite lifting of the corporate veil if the circumstances so warrant. This issue is also closely linked to cross-defaults in financing agreements, which can trigger a group wide crisis.
Insolvency as an Acquisition Model

IBC provides a viable M&A route by offering a "clean slate" that extinguishes liabilities, as established in the Tata Steel's 2018 acquisition of Bhushan Steel, which became the template for CIRP as a discount-priced M&A route, upheld in cases like
Ghanashyam Mishra & Sons v. Edelweiss ARC
JSW Steel's acquisition of Bhushan was meant to be the sequel, until
Kalyani Transco v. Bhushan Power and Steel

(2025) unwound it citing infirmity in the procedures such as non-filing of mandatory Form H eligibility certificate under Section 29A, and JSW delayed implementation for years. This highlights the fact that plan approval is not the end of legal risk and that legal advisors of acquirers must treat procedural hygiene and strict implementation timelines as critical diligence items.
What Does IBC 2.0 Offer
The IBC (Amendment) Act, 2026 represents the distilled wisdom of a decade of implementation experience. Key changes include:
* Specific definitions such as ‘security interest’ and ‘avoidance transactions.
* The Adjudicating Authority must decide applications within 14 days.
* Withdrawal cannot occur before the CoC is constituted.
* A new mechanism allows creditors to initiate insolvency directly, subject to defined approval thresholds and procedural safeguards.
* Extends the role of creditors into the liquidation stage.
* Assets of guarantors to be included in the resolution. Guarantees cannot be enforced during moratorium.
* Phased approval of plans, protects licences and regulatory permissions.

In Conclusion, IBC introduced a sophisticated creditor-driven approach towards financial distress, with a focus on rescue rather than liquidation, highlighting the distinction between whole and ‘sum of all parts.’ The success of IBC has unfortunately been stymied by capacity (tribunal bench strength and infrastructure) falling well short of case volume, frustrating the very objective of timely resolution. Further, the misuse of the framework for recoveries cannot be ignored. However, a decade of implementation has sharpened legal strategies, especially with proactive measures at early signs of distress. It is expected that with its tighter timelines and enhanced accountability, IBC 2.0 will further refine legal practice in this area.
